messages.author: 3965602d3ef7ee78
messages.subject: Boxplots and rounding
parts:
Hey folks,

I'm having a rather curious issue with boxplots rounding the mean of
my dataset to whole numbers (1,2,3,4). For example, I have 3 data
values, with means of 5.6777, 5.092593, and 4.559259. When the
boxplots display, however, the mean line on the graph shows as exactly
6, exactly 5, and exactly 5.

I've tried to reproduce the problem on another data set, without luck.
For example, when I run this on the diamonds data set:

attach(diamonds)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(clarity, depth)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.size=1.5)
+ coord_cartesian(ylim=c(60, 65))
mean(depth)

my eye doesn't see anything incorrect, even when I zoom in very close.

Does anyone have any clues as to why a very similar boxplot command
would be rounding the means of my data?

Here's my full command ---

ggplot(traversed, aes(traversed$testedLang, traversed$intuitiveness))
+ geom_boxplot(outlier.size=1.5) + facet_grid(programmer~.,) +
xlab("") + ylab("Intuitiveness") + coord_cartesian(ylim=c(-0.05,
10.05)) + opts(panel.margin = unit(1, "lines"))

The same holds true even if you remove all but:

ggplot(traversed, aes(traversed$testedLang, traversed$intuitiveness))
+ geom_boxplot(outlier.size=1.5)

In this case, intuitiveness is a numeric and testedLang and programmer
are both factors.

Any clues would be greatly appreciated.

Stefik

messages.author: affa918ed63b6275
messages.subject: Re: Boxplots and rounding
parts:
Hi, the horizontal lines in each box represent median, not mean.
Probably your data consists of integer only, while diamond$depth is
real numeric.

messages.subject: Re: Boxplots and rounding
parts:
> Hi, the horizontal lines in each box represent median, not mean.
> Probably your data consists of integer only, while diamond$depth is
> real numeric.

Oh, right, duh, that makes sense, and is exactly the issue (my data is
integer only). In our case, the differences we found in our study are
relatively small, but statistically significant, and using the median
makes the graphs look incorrect, now that I think about it more
carefully.

Do you think, then, that perhaps we should use confidence intervals,
or some other kind of graph to make the differences more obvious to a
reader?

Thanks. It's such a minor thing, but this helped,

Stefik
